Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Daniel, a 49-year-old North American architect, came to treatment after months of feeling as though the world had become an unsafe place to move through. The event that marked him had not been something he did to anyone, but something he witnessed: a violent attack that unfolded in front of him with such speed and brutality that, even afterward, he struggled to put the sequence back together in his mind. He could remember the force of the violence, the shock of watching it happen, and the immediate bodily wave of nausea that rose in him afterward, but when he tried to tell the story, the pieces would not line up in a clear order. He would begin with what he saw first, then stop, frown, and admit that he knew what happened but could not find the words to describe it properly. At times, while speaking, he seemed to slip back into the scene; his face would tighten and he would say that remembering it made it feel as if it were happening right then, not in the past.

In the weeks after the incident, Daniel noticed that certain smells could bring the event back with alarming force. In the street, in a client’s building, or even in his own home, a related smell would hit him unexpectedly and he would feel suddenly sick, as though his body recognized danger before his mind had time to catch up. He became especially wary in places where he could not immediately see who was around him. In restaurants, meeting rooms, lobbies, and unfamiliar job sites, he was drawn almost automatically to the wall, choosing seats where his back could be protected and he could see the entire room. He described feeling unsafe unless his back was against something solid, with a view of doors and people’s movements. When he entered any room or building, he began scanning for exits without thinking about it, counting them, mapping them, and noting which ones would be easiest to reach. Even when nothing was wrong, he felt jumpy, as if his body were waiting for the next sudden burst of violence. Small noises made him flinch more than they used to, and he was embarrassed by how easily startled he had become.

As an architect, Daniel had once enjoyed moving comfortably through different spaces, observing light, layout, and circulation in a way that felt professional and calm. After the traumatic event, however, his work and daily routine started to narrow around his need to feel oriented and protected. Site visits became taxing because he found himself preoccupied with where he could stand, where he could sit, and how quickly he could leave if something happened. In meetings, he was less likely to take the center chair or sit with his back to the room, and he found himself choosing positions that allowed him to monitor the whole space. He did not describe these changes as dramatic, but they accumulated into a way of living that felt constricted. He and his wife noticed that he was less easy in social settings, more likely to keep to the edge of a gathering, and more likely to leave early than he had been before. Daniel said this made him feel isolated and set apart from other people, as if everyone else still belonged in a world he could no longer fully enter.

He also came to believe, with a persistence he found hard to shake, that there was something about him that had made the event happen. He could not explain this belief in a logical way, and he knew it did not sound fair when he said it aloud, but it remained with him nonetheless. Alongside that belief was a growing sense that bad things could not be stopped from happening to him, no matter how carefully he tried to arrange his surroundings. He found himself checking exits, choosing seats, and watching people’s movements with the uneasy sense that these habits were necessary, yet never enough. Even when he prepared himself, he still felt vulnerable to another sudden threat. His wife had urged him to seek help after noticing how often he avoided crowded places, how tense he became in public, and how exhausted he seemed from constantly watching the room. Daniel himself said that what finally pushed him to make an appointment was the realization that he no longer trusted ordinary places to stay ordinary. He came hoping to understand why the memories would not settle into the past, why his body kept reacting as if danger were still near, and whether he could learn to move through the world without feeling that he was always bracing for the next violent moment.
